title: Robert Taylor and a mysterious woman neighbor
summary: Talk of bad things happening to musicians and a story of a rich red-haired woman she worked near.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Get paralyzed. Do you remember Robert Taylor, the trumpet play? He was supposed to get paralyzed. Yes, indeed. Yes, indeed. I know Robert. He kicked a woman down. She was supposed to fix him.

Yeah, they say that. They say that child. That's what Punch told me. People used to be bad doing things, but I can't get these children to believe nothing like that. That was true. I was scared of everybody and I still am. That's why I don't mix much. And I tried to get them not to mix either. My girl was in California and I didn't rest until I was going out there. I used to tell her, keep women out of your house and be very careful because women is a deceitful, jealous hearted thing. All of them. I used to work for a white woman on Dantese Street. She had everything hard bush. A little bit old short red-haired girl lived in the next apartment, had a room. And she had a car. I don't know, not a big car like they have now, but a little car. Looked like it was a child's play toy. But she come from away with that car. She come from away. She didn't belong here. And she was just as sweet. She used to slip me her undercoded things to do, you know. Always putting something in my hand. I used to do them right along there in the yard with the others, you know. And she got so jealous. She said, I wonder how she lives. She's not working. I wonder how she lives. I said, she ain't around begging either. She said, you know. And she just kept on wandering around. She said, you know something? I said, we oughtn't let her stay in the neighborhood. I said, why? She ain't waste staying in the neighborhood. I said, why? She said, because she's either got my husband or some other decent woman's husband. She said, I'm going to run out of the neighborhood. I said, I wouldn't do that. She ain't doing you nothing. So when I brought her up things, I told her, I said, anything you're doing, you be careful, because these white people are watching you. I said, you white like them, but they don't like them. She was cute little, attractive. She had red hair and she was pretty attractive. She was pretty attractive.

Because I know all them men would look at her because they had to look at her. She was something on the eyes. And she said, Bernie, she said, I'm not stunned about none of them. She said, I'm not doing them nothing. I'm giving them no trouble. And to know, she said, the first one that said anything to me, I'm going to put them in jail for my character. She said, they don't know who I am. I said, that's right. She said, they don't know where I'm from. And she said, they don't see nobody come in my house. They don't see nobody go with me. She said, I go alone. I come alone. I said, you certainly do. She said, you the only person comes here. She said, they better not say nothing than let me in. Or somebody tell me other than you. She said, I wouldn't get you in no trouble. She said, but I'll fix them. So they just kept on, kept on. So Mr. Billy told his wife, she said, now listen. She said, you better stop and let up for that girl. I said, you don't know her. She said, she can cause you a lot of trouble. So you let up with that girl. So finally, they, but they never let her go to nothing. They had invited her, you know. So finally, she just disappeared. She left. I didn't know who she was. I didn't know where she come from here. But she was pretty thin. Come back. Come back.
Come back. She might have been, she might have had money of her own.

I think she did. I think pretty that woman was. Ain't no man let her own. She must have had her husband and they had some separation, you know. And she had money. She was a rich girl and had left home on to her father or something at home. Because she had too many fine clothes and had money up home. She had plenty of money. And she had everything in that little place that you want to eat and drink. All kind of drinks and eats. Give me, go ahead. She'd sit down and I'd go up there and me and her, I'd fix the sandwiches and serve her. She said, you know, boy, do you want to leave here? I said, mm-mm. She said, I'll take you away as my personal maid to wait on me. She said, you understand how to wait on people. She said, I ain't study my them old war suffogates. What the shit? I used to laugh. And they'd be peeping at me. Don't let her see her come. And she had that little bit of feet and that little walk. And that would kill her. I used to tell her, I said, don't ride so much. I said, walk out to catch the Tulane car and let them see you. I said, just walk. I said, they're going to be breaking their necks, peeping, blah, blah.
